story_text.value:
I've been a heavy user of Emacs Org mode for a decade and a half. As AI has reduced how often I'm using a text-editor, I was finding myself tied to spacemacs just for Org, and I was searching for a way to keep those workflows and notes, but be fully decoupled from Emacs. (I blogged about that here: https://avi.press/posts/2024-01-15-standalone-org.html, the original idea for this project).

Today I'm excited to launch Celorga: a portable re-implementation of Org, with no dependency on Emacs or elisp, and adds many primitives so you can use it with all of your agents.

Celorga offers a portable CLI that covers most core Org capabilities like agenda management, structured editing, searching, and more. It also well offers a tons of capabilities for working with all of your agents (any agent, any harness), like an MCP server, and the ability to kick off your agents easily from any TODO in your notes. It offers most capabilities of multi-agent harnesses today, but aimed at a more general workload than just coding.

I believe at this point, Celorga is most polished Org experience outside of Emacs. It comes with native Mac and iOS apps (Linux & android coming soon). Fully OSS, Apache 2.

- GitHub: https://github.com/aviaviavi/celorga

- Homepage: https://celorga.io

- Install the CLI from npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/celorga

Feedback is welcome!

story_text.value:
I've always wanted to play Wing Commander with friends, so we could fly the story missions together. In 2015, I hypothesized that the full game state fit in the data segment (only 64k), and I could do small position and orientation experiments with vbindiff to discover how the memory was organized. Some fun findings: the camera was in entity index 0x3D (a "3D" joke?). My brother, Patrick, figured out Borland's overlay loader crashed the game until we made our stub look like a real stack frame. To play you need your own copy (e.g. the GOG version) and you drag setup.exe into the browser. It's a DOSBox mod: no game files are hosted. We reversed the game by hand, but LLMs were used for the recent browser/peer-to-peer WebRTC with voice chat port recently, and we continue to use them for ongoing work.

I'll be in the lobby for some hours if anyone wants to fly together.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're the co-founders of Acyclic (YC F26).

Acyclic runs any agentic workflow as a swarm. You give it a task and your project; it splits the work across many coding agents, each in its own sandbox, runs them in parallel, and merges what they produce into one patch or pull request.

Our thesis: agentic workflows should be realtime, no matter how complex the task. The bottleneck should be human ideation and design, whilst building happens at the speed of thought.

To bring this to you we make our agents recursively fork and speculative execute. This means that if an agent has 2 independent tasks to do, it will just split into 2 agents to solve both tasks quickly and merge back up the tree. Additionally, for sequential operations we have “speculative” agents which guess the next steps of the workflow as a pre-fetch step.

To make this efficient we are solving the infrastructure bottlenecks. We are solving the memory, communication, routing and durable execution issues. This infra is open source at acyclic.dev/github, so check it out!

To run your own swarm (check out acyclic.dev for a full guide)

``` npm install -g @acyclic-labs/cli acyclic swarm run --task <prompt> --dir <files_to_upload> ```

A good (non-coding) first task to try out: Do deep research into a person. “Do deep research into Jeff Goldblum“ You can view the results at acyclic.dev/dashboard or stream the results back to the cli using:

``` acyclic swarm pull <swarm-id> --apply ```

Check out some more research examples at acyclic.dev/evals, right now our biggest useful swarm is 236 agents for a code migration.

story_text.value:
Hey!

In my spare time I am working on this little tool to let groups vote on accomodation/budget/dates for trips.

I started building it, because the yearly trip with our friends got out of hand before it even started. After a lot of back and forth we were able to decide on date and budget, but the accomodation itself turned out to be a stress test for our friendships. From time to time new links got thrown into the group chat, in between all other messages. In the end we decided for a rather random accomodation, nobody was really happy with.

While our trip in the end turned out to be great - with the right people the accomodation does not matter much - I was convinced a little app could benefit us and maybe others aswell. So I started building WeDecide.

I wanted to achieve the following:

* The focus is on the decision making, not on research.

* It should work in combination with a group chat, not be an all in one tool.

* Everyone in the chat should be easily involved. That means simple UX and no registration. I had doodle in mind for this.

To finance it the app generates affiliate links of a number of hotel platforms. I won't get rich of it!

Some technical details: It's a Nuxt app + postgres db running on a 5€ per month server of a german provider. Additionally I set up Bunny CDN. Tracking is done via a self hosted Plausible instance. Everything is hosted in Europe by European companies.

Feedback is very much welcome and hopefully this tool is useful for somebody!

Cheers

story_text.value:
We've spent 2 years developing Villa (https://villamoves.com), a spatial fitness and gaming product that runs on the Mac and works a bit like VR, but without a headset.

How it works: computer vision senses your full-body motion, running locally on Apple silicon (M1 or later). The music you play generates new gameplay levels (you can play NTS mixtapes or stream your own playlists).

There are seven movement-based games for launch, ranging from tennis to alien combat. In each one, your body is the controller. Villa also features a gesture-based interface, so you control everything touchlessly from across the room.

Here’s 30 seconds of gameplay: https://youtu.be/IyhIom8TgZE

It’s free to download and play (we plan to add subscriptions down the line).

We're Snap and Seene alumni. Happy to answer questions.

story_text.value:
Hi all,

So I have been working on this project KiviDB from February 2026. It started as a project for me to understand rust, having a product with no GC pauses, memory blow up after snapshots and getting OOM on running pods, and that was actually an issue I faced with Dragonfly. I wanted to have something picking the best of Rust, but also picking the best parts of other alternatives like Garnet and Dragonfly. I used AI a lot, but I was the one making the design decisions based on the tests that claude picked from my history of troubleshooting sessions as part of my job. KiviDB supports both RESP2 and RESP3 protocol. I had some founders credits on my AWS account which helped me with the infra, and running instances I could perform benchmark on.

Its keyspace is sharded across threads, it is multi-threaded in nature, and performs best on Linux due to io_uring, I used the tokio_uring crate for this. It also has tokio fallback for other OS's. I hadn't open sourced it until recently as I felt it was not ready yet, the best way to learn it was to build a cloud managed service for it across all three widely used cloud providers i.e AWS, GCP and azure. Since I used to mainly work with cloud, I had some insights on what would be the best ways for the deployments, how to conduct failovers, manage SLAs, etc. And that's what I took help from claude to fast pace it. The website does look like AI slop but it works for now, given my limited resources, that's all I had. You may check it out at : https://kividb.io, I open sourced the core engine under AGPLv3, didn't want to have just source available, because that is available with other tools too. It supports apprx 98-99% of the redis 8.10 commands, few have issues and you can find them at https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues, contributors are welcome.

Now the numbers, for the final benchmark, I used 2 c7gn.metal servers, in the same placement group in us-east1, and I used memtier-benchmark tool for this. The setting was : 10M keys, 100B each, 32 cores in use with both pipeline and un-pipelined runs.

pipeline 16 GET: KiviDB 21.2M ops/sec vs Dragonfly 2.0 9.1M, Redis 8.10 2.4M, Redis Cluster 32 shards 4.7M

When not pipelined, Dragonfly performed slightly better at 3.35M ops/sec vs kividb at 3.07M ops/sec. Memory per key was also slightly worse than dragonfly and almost same as Redis, 177B (kividb) vs 134B (dragonfly) vs 178B (redis).

With vector ingestion times it was slower but when querying, it was faster than most alternatives at lower ef, however slower than dragonfly at high ef. Most of the technical details are mentioned here so you can check it out: https://kividb.io/benchmarks.

easiest way to try it: docker run -d -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb

I am looking forward to building a community around this, provide better rust based tools, I am open to constructive criticism and value informed opinion. Thanks

title.value: Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache

story_text.value:
This is a little thing I built: it's a visually pleasing office with AI agents working on GitHub repositories and submitting pull requests. They are getting issues, reproduce them and then fix them. I was using it privately in a Discord call and many people requested a public open-source version, so I got Claude Opus 5.5 to rewrite the entire code in Rust. It's available as a service on macOS, Linux and Windows.

In my use case I use it to make PRs for ArtCraft, the Adobe Suite clone that is viral right now. This tool got me into the top 10 contributors within 5 days. I have 361 total pull requests, 234 of them got merged. I think that statistic speaks for the quality this thing can achieve. Right now on low usage settings it's round about 51 pulls a day fast, and it does not use up as much usage as you think it would, mainly because the tasks get split between Haiku models on default settings and not everything is running on one big Opus session. Also they get optimal prompts and clear instructions every step, which further reduces token usage. It can also bughunt: about 60% of pulls are code problems the tool found by itself.

If you are a GitHub contributor to any project or want to solve issues on your own repository, this is the tool for you.

title.value: Show HN: ApolloOffice – Local AI workers that turn GitHub issues into tested PRs

story_text.value:
0sql is an open-source semantic layer engine written in Rust. Compared to Cube and Metricflow, here are the major differences:

Partition aware, agg aware, and compute engine aware semantic routing.

Comprehensive suite of measures out of the box.

Snapshot, LOD, compound, ratios, calculations, cross-domain, and run time measure transformations. Automatic data blending across fact domains. Row level security built-in.

Website: https://0sql.io/

Blog post: https://blog.strata.do/p/0sql-is-open-source-now

Please send feedbacks and issues on Github.
